_about: R19 SA: Gentle Gate Animal Sanctuary (plan_sanctuary.js). Every name and line of copy. Local frame: u east, v south from (868, -38).

names.arch2: RESCUE  ·  CARE  ·  A HOME FOR LIFE
names.feed2: the vet clinic at the east end

venue.p: A forever home for animals who needed one: retired ranch horses, donkeys walked in from the desert, goats and sheep from homes that could no longer keep them, desert tortoises, rabbits, hens and two owls who cannot fly free again. Everything here runs on care that people give: their time, their hands, a bale of hay, a morning of mucking out. Walk in, say hello at the Welcome Barn, and feed someone at the fence.

troughs.k: Galvanised stock tanks, filled every morning
troughs.p: Clean water is the first thing a rescued animal gets and the last thing a volunteer checks before the barn lights go down. The tanks are scrubbed on Saturdays by whoever turns up. There are no ponds here on purpose: in the high desert, water belongs in a trough where it stays clean and nobody gets stuck.

horses.p: Juniper, Dusty and Ranger worked cattle for most of their lives. Pepper, Biscuit and Moe arrived thin and footsore from the open desert. They share the run-in shed, the round bale and a lot of opinions. Stand at the rail and press E: they know what a visitor means.

goats.k: Spools, a deck and plenty of hay
goats.p: Goats climb, so the yard has cable spools and a plank deck to stand on; the sheep prefer the shade and the hay rack. Clover is the boss, Woolsey is the gentlest, and every one of them will tell you it has not been fed today.

tortoise.k: Burrows, basking stones and slow afternoons
tortoise.p: Old Sage, Pebble and Mesa were surrendered by families who could no longer care for them. A tortoise can outlive the people who adopt it, so this garden is built for decades: deep burrows for the heat, flat stones for the morning sun, and greens at ten o'clock sharp.

hutch.p: Thistle, Nutmeg, Button and Fern share the yard with four hens who run it. The hutches are raised against the heat and the coop has a ramp the hens ignore. Volunteers sit on the straw corner on quiet mornings so the shy ones learn that hands bring good things.

aviary.k: Two owls and a covey of quail
aviary.p: Hoot and Luna are great horned owls who were hurt too badly to hunt again. They live here with a covey of quail under a shade roof and a dead mesquite full of perches. Go in quietly through the double door: the owls will watch you the whole way round.

feed.k: Hay to the rafters, the vet clinic at the east end
feed.p: Every bale stacked in here was given by somebody, a neighbour with a trailer, a school food drive, a volunteer who skipped a weekend away. The clinic at the east end is where Dr. Okafor checks hooves, teeth and weights, and where new arrivals rest before they meet the herd.

hay.p: Horses and donkeys eat hay all day, goats pick the best bits, and the rest becomes bedding. A sanctuary measures the year in bales. Sit on one if you like: they are made for it.

talk.t: Welcome to Gentle Gate. I'm Marisol, I run the place, which mostly means I count bales and answer to a donkey named Pepper. Everyone who lives here came because someone noticed them and decided to help.

A sanctuary is a promise: once an animal comes through that gate, it has a home for the rest of its life. No shows, no rides, just care. The horses retired from ranch work, the donkeys walked in from the desert, the tortoises were handed in by families who loved them but could not keep them.

The same way everyone here does: give a little of what you have. An hour with a muck fork. A bale of hay. Sponsoring one resident on the adoption board on the porch. Giving is not only money, it is showing up, and care is the most honest kind of giving there is.

Feed somebody at a fence (press E at the rail), read the adoption board on the porch, and talk to Teo about a volunteer morning. Dr. Okafor is in the clinic in the feed barn if you want to see how the residents are looked after.

greet: Mind the stall, Moe is napping.

talk.t: Hello, I'm Dr. Okafor. Every resident gets a check-up here: hooves, teeth, eyes, weight. Old animals need small, steady care far more than they need anything dramatic.

A donkey's hooves trimmed every eight weeks. A tortoise weighed before and after winter. An owl's diet weighed to the gram. It is quiet, patient work, and it only happens because people keep giving their time and their hay.
Moe, in the recovery stall. He came in with sore feet and a bad attitude. The feet are better. The attitude is a work in progress. Go and say hello to the herd for him.
Hey! I'm Teo, I look after the volunteers and the adoption board. We run on helpers: mornings are mucking out and water, afternoons are hay and brushing, evenings are the barn check.

Every resident has a card. Sponsoring one means you look out for them: you visit, you bring their favourite greens, you help with their care day. The animal stays here, safe, for life. You just become part of their family.
Brilliant. Grab a pair of gloves from the barn and start at the troughs. And take a look at the board on the wall: pick a resident and get to know them.

adopt.kicker: press E to read the board
adopt.title: Sponsor a resident
adopt.sub: Every name here was given a second chance by someone who cared

talk.t: Six cards pinned to the cork, each with a photograph and a name. Across the top in green paint: SPONSOR A RESIDENT. Underneath, smaller: nobody here is for sale, and nobody leaves.

PEPPER, donkey. Walked in out of the desert two winters ago with overgrown hooves and no name. Now the loudest voice in the yard at feeding time. Likes: carrots, ear scratches, being right. Needs: a hoof trim every eight weeks.

HOOT, great horned owl. Found with a broken wing beside the runway road. The wing healed, but not well enough to hunt. Likes: the high branch, dusk, staring. Needs: a weighed supper every evening and a quiet aviary.

THISTLE, rabbit. Handed in when her family moved. Shy for a month, now the first to the gate when the greens come. Likes: dandelion leaves, the straw corner, gentle hands. Needs: a cool hutch and company.

OLD SAGE, desert tortoise. Older than the barn. Lived in one backyard for forty years until the family could no longer care for him. Likes: the morning stone, hibiscus, taking his time. Needs: a burrow and a lot of patience.

Your name goes on the card in pencil. Sponsoring means care, not ownership: you visit, you help on their care day, you bring their favourite greens, and you tell people about them. That is how a place like this keeps its gate open, one giver at a time.
